title: Cross-Domain Joint-Embedding Pretraining For Heterogeneous Industrial Time Series
abstract: Industrial predictive maintenance and manufacturing tasks frequently contain abundant sensor measurements, but with limited labeled data. We investigate cross-domain self-supervised pretraining using joint-embedding predictive architecture for heterogeneous industrial time series (JEPA-HITS), which learns one encoder from various domains such as battery, semiconductor chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), computer numerical control (CNC) machining, and bearing while preserving dataset-specific temporal scales. We evaluate representation reuse on regression and classification problems under reduced-label downstream training, and leave-one-domain-out (LODO) pretraining. Compared with the same architecture initialized randomly, LODO pretraining reduces RMSE from 10.72 to 7.95 on battery remaining useful life (RUL), 4.34 to 3.89 on CMP, and 13.53 to 11.72 on tool wear regression, while improving bearing fault diagnosis macro-F1 from 0.547 to 0.737. Overall results suggest that unlabeled time series measurements from heterogeneous industrial processes can provide reusable representations for downstream learning with limited labeled data.

title: Training Autoregressive Language Models on Rounded, Bounded, and Censored Numerical Labels via Exact Likelihood
abstract: Numerical labels often specify a set of possible values: a measurement is rounded, a laboratory test reports only a bound, or a program is stopped at a timeout. We introduce boundary marginalization, the first method that trains an autoregressive language model on the exact likelihood of such observations through its existing digit tokens. A fixed-width, order-preserving numeral representation groups consecutive grid values under shared digit prefixes. An interval is a union of such groups, so its exact probability and gradient follow from at most two boundary paths, the successive digit prefixes of its endpoints, each of length logarithmic in the number of grid values. The resulting objective unifies precise, rounded, bounded, and censored supervision and trains digit decisions at the resolution supplied by each observation. The same computation supports exact distributional queries and unbiased gradients for the continuous ranked probability score on exact labels. Experiments show recovery of a conditional distribution from rounded and censored reports alone, improved likelihood on naturally censored molecular measurements, and more accurate code latency distributions on two backbones. Exact interval updates remain tractable as the numerical support grows to one million values.

title: Moiré reconstruction at a twisted SrTiO3 interface
abstract: Twisted oxide double layers have emerged as a promising platform for exploring moiré physics, including polar topologies and emergent electronic phases. However, the intrinsic complexity of oxide surfaces, such as contamination, roughness, and the presence of two distinct terminations (AO and BO2), can complicate the identification of buried interfacial structures. Here, using atomically flat SrTiO3 membranes with a predominantly SrO-TiO2 interfacial configuration, we directly visualize a moiré-periodic structural reconstruction at the buried interface that is distinct from the geometric moiré of rigid stacking. The reconstructed interface hosts head-to-head-like polar distortions, moiré-modulated Ti electronic structure, and enhanced microwave admittance in otherwise paraelectric and insulating SrTiO3. Our work demonstrates that, with a well-defined termination, moiré reconstruction could serve as a route to emergent electrical behavior in twisted perovskite oxides.

title: Turbo-GMM: FlashAttention-Inspired GPU-Accelerated Gaussian Mixture Model
abstract: Expectation-maximization (EM) for Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) requires scoring $N$ data points against $K$ mixture components. Prior fused GPU implementations, notably Flash-GMM, eliminate materialization of the $N \times K$ responsibility matrix but traverse the component dimension twice to compute normalization terms and accumulate sufficient statistics. We introduce Turbo-GMM, a single-sweep fused EM kernel that completes responsibility normalization and sufficient-statistic accumulation within one traversal of the component dimension. By retaining the complete component axis on chip, Turbo-GMM avoids the second score computation required by the released two-sweep Flash-GMM implementation. Its applicability is limited by register pressure, occupancy, and the component and feature dimensions, making it particularly suitable for large datasets with relatively small numbers of components. For larger configurations, Turbo-GMM employs a two-pass fallback following the established fused design. We establish algebraic equivalence to standard EM in real arithmetic and evaluate sixteen configurations on an NVIDIA A100. Under the reported benchmarking protocol, Turbo-GMM achieves a median $2.15\times$ speedup over the evaluated Flash-GMM implementation and up to $5.3\times$ and $9.9\times$ over PyTorch and \texttt{scikit-learn}, respectively. The results demonstrate the potential of single-sweep component traversal while identifying on-chip resource constraints as the principal limitation of this approach.

title: Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential for the Mo-S-Al-O System
abstract: We develop a machine-learned neuroevolution potential (NEP) for the Mo-S-Al-O system, targeting MoS$_2$ heteroepitaxy on c-plane sapphire, $α$-Al$_2$O$_3$(0001). The potential is trained on 63,611 PBE+D3 structures distilled from about 1.1 million curated density-functional-theory (DFT) configurations, using an energy-difference loss function that directly targets interfacial and orientation-dependent energies. On held-out data, the energy and force errors are 29 meV/atom and 0.23 eV/$\mathring{A}$. Validated against DFT on a suite of physical properties, the NEP reproduces the lattice constants within 0.3 %, the elastic constants within 17 %, the phonon dispersions with mean deviations below 2.5%, and the surface energies within 1.3 %. At the MoS$_2$/sapphire interface, it reproduces the adhesion energy minimum within 0.8 %, the interfacial energy within 2.2 % and the most stable orientation of the monolayer. It preserves the DFT-predicted energetic ordering of edges, point defects (Spearman $ρ$ = 0.995) and mirror-twin boundaries ($ρ$ = 1.0), and reproduces tilt grain-boundary energies within 8 % ($ρ$ = 0.98) and stacking-fault energy barriers within 14 %. The resulting potential enables future studies of the atomic-scale mechanisms of defect formation in two-dimensional heteroepitaxy.

title: One Mistake, Three Layers: Persistence Rules Under Depth Correlation
abstract: Probing frozen representations layer by layer is now standard practice, but reporting when a signal first becomes decodable requires a rule for reading a depth curve, and the obvious rule is wrong. On synthetic curves with known ground truth, requiring a probe score to exceed a null-calibrated threshold for three consecutive stages reports an onset nineteen stages early under transformer-like depth correlation, with every resample returning an onset. The failure follows from correlation between neighboring layers, a hazard known in neuroimaging but not, to our knowledge, checked for depth curves. We give an estimator whose error rate is calibrated rather than assumed. Null trajectories are built by permuting labels within each evaluation unit and holding each permutation fixed across depth, preserving the correlation structure the rule must survive; thresholds are per-layer order statistics; and the persistence requirement is calibrated rather than chosen. Applied to pocket information in a frozen co-folding trunk, stratifying 1,820 post-cutoff targets by protein-family and pocket familiarity, the five-stage rule fires on 4 to 7 per cent of null trajectories against a nominal 5 per cent and the three-stage rule on 12 to 17: the synthetic failure reproduces on real data. Pocket membership is decodable above threshold at all 48 blocks in all four regimes, so the onset cannot discriminate them; the pre-declared accumulation depth does, and is latest for familiar families with structurally novel pockets in every feature set. That regime is also the weakest, by a margin surviving controls for length, pocket measure and alignment depth. Separately, a widely used public co-folding checkpoint loads against its own code with 128 trunk parameters missing; those would be randomly initialized, and every representation extracted would be partly noise while appearing normal.

title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
abstract: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

title: Early-age formation of MgO-SiO$_2$ binders and the effect of hydromagnesite and dehydrated hydromagnesite: An in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction and pair distribution function study
abstract: MgO-SiO$_2$ binders are promising low-CO$_2$ alternatives to Portland cement that can permanently store CO$_2$ by incorporating magnesium carbonate phases. Adding a magnesium carbonate such as nesquehonite or hydromagnesite is known to change the initial hydration product from crystalline brucite (Mg(OH)$_2$) to disordered hydrous carbonate-containing brucite (HCB), yet how these binders evolve during the initial hours of reaction remains largely unknown. Here, in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis follows an MgO-SiO$_2$ paste with and without hydromagnesite (HY, Mg$_5$(CO$_3$)$_4$(OH)$_2$$\cdot$4H$_2$O) or dehydrated hydromagnesite (DHY, HY heated at 325 °C to remove water) over the first 24 h, with ex situ measurements to 42 days. Real space phase quantification reveals that magnesium-silicate-hydrate (M-S-H) is detected in the first scan (~45 min) of every paste, before formation of any brucite or HCB. The PDF results also show that in the neat MgO-SiO$_2$ paste, half of the M-S-H present at 42 days has formed by 24 h, while no M-S-H is detected by XRD at any age due to the intrinsic disorder present in this phase. Both carbonate sources (HY and DHY) are found to increase the extent of MgO dissolution, where no unreacted MgO is detected at 24 h in contrast with >7 days for the neat paste. However, DHY is seen to slow the initial stages of MgO dissolution (prior to ~6 h) compared with the neat paste, a period during which significant DHY rehydration is seen to occur without any HCB formation. Hence, this investigation shows that the onset of HCB precipitation in MgO-SiO$_2$-(D)HY paste is influenced by the hydration state of the DHY phase, where precipitation is delayed while DHY is rehydrating.

title: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024-2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model's signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t = 1.7) on the blinded January-July 2026 test. The commercial models' readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.

title: Characterisation of surface layers formed on plasma-facing components in controlled fusion devices: Role of heavy ion elastic recoil detection
abstract: Wall components retrieved from the TEXTOR tokamak after tracer experiments with nitrogen-15 and molybdenum hexafluoride (MoF6) injection were studied to determine deposition patterns and, by this, to conclude on material migration. Toroidal limiter tiles made of carbon fibre composites and fine grain graphite were examined using time-of-flight heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis. Molybdenum deposition patterns indicated migration based on erosion and prompt re-deposition. Nitrogen-15 was trapped together with the deposited molybdenum. Some information on the depth distribution of species in the top 400 nm layer of the limiters was obtained; however surface roughness of the samples strongly limited resolution. In the case of molybdenum, the largest concentration was found in the 100 nm outermost layer, whereas fluorine and nitrogen-15 displayed more irregular profiles. Other species, besides deuterium fuel and carbon-12, were also identified: boron-10 and boron-11 originating from boronisations, carbon-13 from earlier tracer experiments, nitrogen-14 from plasma edge cooling and metals eroded from the Inconel wall.

title: Deriving benchmark doses for nano- and microplastic-induced neurotoxicity: A systematic tiered framework for fragmented toxicological evidence
abstract: The rapid proliferation of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) has intensified concerns about their potential neurotoxicity, yet heterogeneous, fragmented toxicological evidence limits quantitative human health risk assessment. Here, a structured, two-phase framework is presented that integrates systematic evidence synthesis with Bayesian benchmark dose (BMD) modeling to derive defensible toxicological benchmarks from mammalian oral exposure studies. Neurotoxicity is used as a proof-of-concept case study within a broader, scalable approach.

title: Automatic Generation of Novel Highly-Functional Molecular Sequences
abstract: While multiple methods now exist to generate functional sequence variants from existing annotated examples, it is unclear how well such methods can be used to generate sequences that exceed the functionality of those contained in the example set. Using two complete fitness landscapes, we quantify how effectively generative tools can search sequence space and find rare, novel, highly functional sequences, focusing on variational auto-encoders and information-theoretic methods. We find that an information-theoretic method that does not require training and runs significantly faster than standard Machine-Learning/Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) methods also is significantly more effective in finding rare highly-functional sequences. We discuss the application of this novel method to discover rare polypeptides with anti-bacterial properties that are specific to bacterial, but not eukaryotic, cell membranes.

title: Tracing the Scientific Discovery Capacity of LLMs to Their Training Data
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise for scientific discovery, yet basic questions remain about what enables reliable discovery. How can we trace the scientific discovery capacity of LLMs to their training data? We study this question as one of missing probability mass and develop a theoretical account in which monofacts-the facts observed once during training-set the discovery capacity. In materials science and regulatory genomics, we directly manipulate monofact rates in training sets and find that more monofacts consistently yield more discoveries across two open-weight model families, sampling strategies, and reasoning budgets. Further experiments show the relationship cannot be explained by training-set diversity alone and can transfer across scientific domains when paired with in-domain data. Together, our results identify monofact rate in training data as a key factor governing discoveries in language models.

title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VI. Surface diffusion on a nonmetal-terminated surface
abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate surface diffusion of adsorbates on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs (-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb (-1-1-1) surfaces. The mixed coverage consists of Ga adatoms in the first layer with a nonmetal atom attached above them forming a triangular-based pyramid. The pyramidal structures are stable during surface jumps involving rotations around one of the basal Ga adatoms. Thus, the diffusion proceeds via rotation (pivot) of the pair of the other basal Ga adatoms around an immobile Ga adatom moving them into new, originally empty sites. Using an energy-path determination procedure, the diffusion barriers were obtained as the difference between the initial site energy and the activated complex state energy. The detachment energy of the NM adatom was obtained assuming a final state in atomic and molecular form. The energy barrier for detachment to the atomic state is high for all atoms, on the order of 5 eV. For the molecular state these barriers are different: smaller for nitrogen, on the order of 1 eV, which is related to the high dissociation energy of the N2 molecule. For P and As the barrier is above 2 eV. For Sb it was not determined. Accordingly, the surface diffusion length is macroscopically large, indicating that all NM adatoms arrive at the steps.

title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VII. Step kinetics
abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate the kinetics of attachment of new segments of the crystalline lattice (pyramids) at steps on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs(-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb(-1-1-1) surfaces. Diffusion species are gallium adatoms at high coverage or gallium adatoms connected with nonmetal atom creating stable pyramids. These pyramids arrive at the steps, and cannot be attached be directly because the Ga adatom at the pyramid base cannot be attached directly. Therefore they are incorporated into the step by additional nonmetal atoms glue atoms arriving from the vapor or detached from other segments of the surface terraces.

title: Human-Supervised Artificial Intelligence Researchers in Electric Power Systems: Knowledge, Physics, Simulation, and Governance for Large Language Models
abstract: Conclusions in power-system research require a clear evidential basis. Researchers need to understand the data sources, modelling assumptions, and solution procedures to assess the conditions under which a conclusion holds. Large language models (LLMs) can help researchers extract information from documents and translate research requests into code and tool calls, but their outputs still require physical validation. Focusing on human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) researchers, this review examines power-system LLM applications and related scientific workflows, together with physics-grounded power AI studies, to discuss the conditions for using LLMs in scientific research. In the proposed knowledge-physics-simulation-governance framework, LLMs translate information and coordinate tasks, simulators and validation tools test models, and experts retain authority over critical assumptions, safety boundaries, and final conclusions. Research processes should preserve materials for review so that claims can be traced to their sources, computations can be reproduced, and failed attempts and approvals can be examined. On this basis, a staged development roadmap and requirements for research reporting are proposed. Evaluation should focus on research artifacts and their validation to assess whether LLMs can improve the efficiency of power-system research within clearly defined permissions.

title: High-Entropy A-Site Disorder Enhances Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity and Stability in Nickelate Thin Films
abstract: Rare-earth nickelates are among the most active oxide electrocatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), owing to their tunable Ni-O covalency, near-unity eg occupancy, and sensitivity to A-site chemistry, oxygen stoichiometry, and epitaxial strain. Here, we use epitaxial A-site high-entropy (La0.2Pr0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2Eu0.2)NiO3 thin films to reveal how epitaxial strain influences defect formation, Ni valence, electronic structure, and OER activity in a chemically disordered rare-earth (RE) sublattice. Tensile strain promotes Ruddlesden-Popper fault formation, interrupts the corner-sharing NiO6 network, and lowers the average Ni oxidation state. Although the occupied density of states near the Fermi level remains largely unchanged, O K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy reveals increased low-energy unoccupied states under tensile strain. First-principles calculations suggest that tensile strain shifts RE 4f-derived states toward the Fermi level, enhancing RE 4f-O 2p-Ni 3d hybridization. These coupled structural and electronic changes lead to earlier OER onset, stronger pre-catalytic Ni redox features, and higher activity than compressively strained films and representative single-A-site nickelates. The high-entropy nickelate also shows enhanced resistance to OER-induced structural degradation compared with LaNiO3. These results suggest that A-site configurational disorder and epitaxial strain can jointly tune defect formation and rare-earth-derived electronic states, providing a route for improving perovskite oxide electrocatalysts.

title: Long-PDE4D degradation attenuates left ventricular cardiomyocyte hypertrophic remodelling
abstract: Spatial compartmentalisation enables cyclic AMP (cAMP) to regulate distinct cellular functions, yet selectively targeting disease-associated signalling remains challenging. Phosphodiesterases constrain local cAMP responses, but conventional inhibitors offer limited isoform selectivity. Here we investigate whether targeted degradation of long phosphodiesterase-4D (PDE4D) isoforms can suppress pathological growth while preserving contractile function. Using adult rat and human ventricular cardiomyocytes and human myocardial slices, we show that the proteolysis-targeting chimera KTX-184 enhances compartmentalised cAMP signalling and attenuates hypertrophic remodelling. In rat cardiomyocytes, KTX-184 increases {beta}-adrenergic cAMP responses in the cytosol and at the plasma membrane, including T-tubule and crest regions, and enhances nuclear protein kinase A activity. In contrast, phospholamban- and ryanodine receptor-associated cAMP nanodomains, calcium transients and sarcomere shortening remain unchanged. KTX-184 prevents angiotensin II-induced hypertrophic remodelling, preserves T-tubule organisation and normalises hypertrophic marker expression. In human cardiomyocytes, it increases cytosolic cAMP responses and prevents overload-induced hypertrophy in myocardial slices. These findings identify long PDE4D isoforms as targets for spatially selective modulation of cAMP signalling and support targeted degradation as an approach to suppress cardiac hypertrophy without increasing contractility.

title: Molecular dinitrogen anions pave the way for low-temperature ammonia synthesis
abstract: While ammonia (NH₃) is best known for its role in fertilizer production, it is attracting attention as a carbon-free hydrogen carrier, potentially offering a practical way to store and transport clean fuel. Despite this promise, NH₃ synthesis still depends on high-temperature, high-pressure processes that are difficult to scale up sustainably. The reason behind this is the extremely strong bond between nitrogen atoms in nitrogen gas (N₂), which requires a lot of energy to break.

title: Disentanglement of interfacial electric fields and electrochemical potential gradients reveals a multidimensional kinetic landscape
abstract: Electrochemical reactions occur at solid–liquid interfaces, where the applied electrochemical potential gradient can act as thermodynamic driving force but can also induce interfacial polarization. A key question has long been how local changes in the chemical potentials of the electrons and the associated excess charge and electric fields impact catalyst kinetics. Here we combine temperature-dependent current transients from oxidative CO stripping with a CO coverage-dependent potential of zero total charge and Raman spectroscopy. We observe a reduction of the activation energy with increasing driving force. By contrast, increasing the distance between the applied potential and the potential of zero total charge results in an increase in the apparent activation energy, which we ascribe to an electric field effect in the double layer. More generally, the results demonstrate how interfacial changes in the chemical potentials give rise to a multidimensional kinetic landscape, in which single-descriptor kinetics fail to capture the nature of the overpotential.

title: Diffusion-Gating Enabled Ternary C2H4 Purification and Inverse C2H2/CO2 Separation in an Adaptive Hopf-Link Metal–Organic Framework
abstract: The simultaneous purification of polymer-grade ethylene (C2H4) and recovery of high-purity acetylene (C2H2) from complex ternary mixtures with carbon dioxide (CO2) represents a critical industrial challenge. Conventional adsorbents employ thermodynamic selectivity to bind C2H2 and CO2 preferentially over C2H4, enabling one-step C2H4 purification but necessitating an energy-intensive desorption step for C2H2 recovery, as C2H2 typically binds more strongly.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Agentic inverse design of spatially programmed materials
abstract: Spatially programmed functional materials, from functionally graded alloys and metamaterials to quantum superlattices, use their spatial structure to tailor physical properties. However, translating a desired spatial structure into a practical fabrication recipe remains challenging due to the complex relationship between processing conditions and resulting material structures. Here we show that a large language model (LLM) agent can inverse-design such fabrication recipes by using a physics-based simulator of ion-matter interactions as a tool. Given an arbitrary depth profile of implanted ions or vacancies, the agent selects the ion species, energies, incident angles, and target material layers; writes, runs, and interprets simulations; and iteratively refines the recipe until the simulated profile matches the target, with minimal human input. Our work demonstrates physics-guided agentic inverse design as a practical approach to making the spatial structure of materials a programmable variable, opening new opportunities to explore emergent physical phenomena and functional phases of matter.

title: Quantifying out-of-distribution data severity with Wasserstein distances: benchmarking large language models for alloy property prediction
abstract: As general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs), such as Gemini and DeepSeek, exhibit increasingly advanced reasoning capabilities, a critical question arises: how do their property prediction abilities compare to those of domain-specific pretrained materials models? In this study, we evaluate predictions for Ti, steels, high-entropy alloy (HEA) and Al, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs surprisingly outperform SteelBERT, MatSciBERT, and SciBERT. To further enhance performance, we introduce a hybrid approach that utilizes numerical priors from a prior model, such as CatBoost or SteelBERT, to guide the general LLMs (Deepseek V3.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash). By inputting these initial estimates from a prior model as prompts, the LLM acts as a reasoning corrector, achieving accuracy superior to the prior model and "unguided mode". Furthermore, we investigate the impact of data strategy using a similarity-based metric, revealing that data quality dominates quantity; using merely 5% of high-similarity reference data of training set as input yields performance similar to the results of using 100% of training set. Additionally, the LLMs demonstrate excellent uncertainty calibration, where self-reported "high" confidence strongly correlates with minimal deviation from ground truth. Our findings suggest that synergizing general-purpose LLMs with prior model numerical baselines and high-quality data curation creates a cost-effective and accurate paradigm for materials discovery, reducing the need for expensive domain-specific pretraining.

title: Current-Confined Formation of a Buried Ge/Si Free Surface for Defect Filtering
abstract: Lattice-mismatched heteroepitaxy is limited by misfit dislocations, threading defects, and residual strain generated at buried interfaces. Here, we show that current-confined electrochemistry transforms the Ge/Si heterointerface into a laterally continuous nanometric free surface while preserving the Ge epilayer. A low-doped Ge layer on a conductive p-type Si substrate redirects anodization current toward the misfit-dislocation-rich interface. Numerical modelling including charge-transfer kinetics shows that this confinement arises from hole-limited charge transfer and, together with electrochemical calibration, defines a process window that combines interfacial current confinement with controlled Si porosification. STEM reveals an approximately 15 Ang separation, while EDX shows localized interfacial oxygen enrichment. After soft annealing, geometric phase analysis and plan-view TEM show a modified strain-relaxation pathway and strongly suppressed threading-dislocation emergence. Raman spectroscopy indicates a reduction in residual tensile strain from approximately 0.10 % to 0.05 %, whereas spreading resistance profiling confirms preservation of the Ge carrier profile. Current-confined electrochemistry therefore provides a controllable post-epitaxial route for buried-interface decoupling, defect filtering, and strain control in lattice-mismatched semiconductor heterostructures.

title: Collective dipole effects amplify field-driven ion transport in amorphous Li$_3$PO$_4$
abstract: Amorphous solid electrolytes often outperform their crystalline counterparts, but how disorder shapes ionic transport under strong electric fields is poorly understood. We use molecular dynamics with a machine-learned interatomic potential and a machine-learned Born-effective-charge model to measure Li mobility in amorphous Li$_3$PO$_4$ and in a crystal with Li vacancies, from the linear to the strongly nonlinear regime. The amorphous phase shows a much stronger field enhancement, and we trace this to a collective dipole effect. The migrating ion carries the same charge in both phases. Alone it would not make the amorphous phase respond more strongly. What makes the difference is the environment. In the amorphous network the surrounding atoms move with the hop. Their motion makes the work the field performs vary widely between hops. Since hopping rates grow exponentially with the work, the most strongly assisted hops can dominate the drift. Disorder thus enhances field-driven transport through the environment rather than the carrier itself, a mechanism that may operate in disordered ion conductors in general.

title: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulation with external field
abstract: Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations with classical path approximation (CPA-NAMD) cannot simulate the carrier dynamics under an external field. We develop CPA-NAMD-extF, a first-principles density-matrix framework for calculating field-driven electronic responses along precomputed finite-temperature ionic trajectories. The method combines explicit external-field coupling with self-consistent updates of electronic density while retaining the computational efficiency of the classical-path approximation. Benchmarks against regular TDDFT methods show close agreement for time-dependent dipoles, finite-field currents, and linear optical responses. Applications to the linear absorption spectrum of crystalline and amorphous SiO$_2$ demonstrate its capability to large and structurally complex systems. This method is also applied to the 2D hybrid perovskite $(\mathrm{BA})_2\mathrm{CsPb}_2\mathrm{Br}_7$. Finite-temperature calculations show that the second-order opto-current response is strongly affected by structural fluctuations. Real-space DC current density further reveals pronounced Br-centered vortex currents, and its microscopic origin is investigated.

title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks
abstract: Current methods of deriving ultrastiff isotropic metamaterials require heuristics or topology optimization, which are highly inefficient and limited by human input. To circumvent this, Physics Informed Neural Networks are applied to analytical equations to systematically solve for plate orientations in closed cell lattices. Following a standardized procedure, the plate orientations were modelled and assembled into geometries resembling quasi random foams for validation via finite element simulations. Closed cell 6-plate geometries were also additively manufactured using LAPIS and experimentally characterized. The results indicate that a minimum of 6 plates is required to constitute an ultrastiff isotropic lattice, 7 plates would return the established plate Cubic Octet structure while 8 to 10 plate geometries did not show significant differences in properties. Despite the introduction of some plate bending due to sub-optimal plate placement strategy, relative stiffness of the PINNs lattices adheres closely to the Hashin Shtrikman upper bound, 90 percent of Hashin Shtrikman upper bound at a relative density of 0.4, and the lattices maintain near isotropic behaviour, achieving a Zener ratio of 0.95 at a relative density of 0.1. Benchmarking results show that specific stiffness of PINNs lattices is higher than the majority of isotropic architectures reported in the literature.

title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.

title: High-resolution relaxometry suggests the presence of pervasive nano-second sugar motions in a DNA duplex.
abstract: Nucleic acids are central to many biomolecular processes central to cellular life, yet characterising their molecular motions and fluctuations with atomic resolution remains challenging. We introduce high-resolution relaxometry, combined with high-field nuclear spin relaxation, as a powerful tool to probe motions in nucleic acids. After recording an extensive spin-relaxation dataset from 2 to 23 T, we propose a framework, within the model-free approach, that allowed us to identify motions occurring both on the picosecond and low nanosecond time scales.

title: Structure of influenza D virus NS1 reveals a novel Zn-binding site and ssRNA-binding activity
abstract: Influenza D virus (IDV) is an emerging pathogen associated with bovine respiratory disease and has potential for zoonotic transmission. Although nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) is a major virulence factor in influenza A and B viruses, the structure and function of IDV NS1 remain poorly defined. Here, we determined crystal structures of the IDV NS1 N-terminal RNA-binding domain (NTD) and C-terminal effector domain (CTD). The NTD retains the conserved homodimeric six-helix fold, whereas the CTD adopts a distinct architecture containing a novel Zn2+-binding site.

title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.

title: Molecular Curvature Enables Tubular π-Stacked Pathways in Three-Dimensional Conductive Metal-Organic Frameworks
abstract: Conductive metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are commonly constructed from planar aromatic ligands, whose geometries favor conventional π-stacking arrangements. However, intrinsically twisted ligands offer an alternative geometric approach to directing aromatic packing and constructing unconventional framework architectures. Here, we employ intrinsically twisted, butterfly-shaped dibenzo[g,p]chrysene-2,3,6,7,10,11,14,15-octaol (DBC) ligands to construct a series of lanthanide MOFs. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals an interpenetrated three-dimensional framework in which π-π interactions between the aromatic fragments generate axially extended tubular π-stacked pathways, alongside one-dimensional channels rich in hydrogen-bonding sites. Lanthanide substitution preserves the overall tubular framework topology while modulating aromatic stacking distances and local pore environments. PrDBC single crystals exhibit mixed electron-proton transport, with electron and proton conductivities reaching 1.62 x 10-3 and 4.37 x 10-4 S cm-1, respectively, at 338 K and 30% relative humidity. This work highlights molecular curvature as a structural design strategy for constructing three-dimensional conductive MOFs that integrate tubular aromatic stacks with tunable pore environments for mixed electron-proton transport.

title: Anion Engineering Enables Concurrent Optimization of Phonon and Carrier Transport in AMg$_2$X$_2$ Zintl Thermoelectrics
abstract: The simultaneous suppression of lattice heat transport and enhancement of carrier transport is central to the development of high-performance thermoelectric materials. Here, we investigate the microscopic mechanisms governing phonon and carrier transport in CaAl$_2$Si$_2$-type AMg$_2$X$_2$ (A = Ca, Sr, Ba; X = P, As, Sb, Bi) Zintl compounds using first-principles calculations, machine-learning interatomic potentials, and Boltzmann transport theory. As X changes from P to Bi, the widening phonon band gap restricts three-phonon scattering channels and increases the relative importance of four-phonon processes. In CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$ and BaMg$_2$Bi$_2$, four-phonon scattering dominates the relaxation of low-frequency heat-carrying modes at 900 K. The Bi-based series also exhibits an anomalous increase in lattice thermal conductivity from Ca to Ba despite the increasing cation mass. Mode-resolved analysis links the lower thermal conductivity of CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$ to reduced low-frequency group velocities and stronger anharmonic scattering, with Ca-related mid-frequency vibrations providing additional four-phonon scattering channels. Including both particle-like and coherent contributions, its lattice thermal conductivity reaches 0.23 W$\cdot$m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ at 900 K. Meanwhile, the increasing covalent character of the vertical Mg-X bonds is accompanied by enhanced band-edge dispersion and reduced carrier effective masses. These electronic changes, together with conduction-band convergence, favor n-type transport and yield a predicted peak $ZT$ of 3.68 at 900 K in CaMg$_2$Bi$_2$. These results elucidate the interplay of phonon spectral structure and higher-order anharmonicity in thermal transport, alongside the distinct electronic response to anion substitution.

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

title: Cage-enforced i-wave altermagnetism in boron-carbon clathrates
abstract: The spin splitting of an altermagnet arises from a rotation that relates its two magnetic sublattices. In known cases it is fixed by the crystal structure. Here we show that guest-host frameworks separate the two roles. In the boron-carbon clathrates $M$B$_3$C$_3$ the ordered cage removes the translation between the two guest sites and enforces cubic $i$-wave altermagnetism, with six symmetry-enforced nodal planes, for any magnetic guest in the compensated state; strain retunes the class to $d$- or $g$-wave. We demonstrate the platform with GdB$_3$C$_3$: its compensated antiferromagnetic ground state is a narrow-gap semiconductor with spin splitting of 0.19 eV at the conduction-band edge, and its weakly pinned Néel vector switches the helicity-resolved optical response on and off according to the magnetic point group. Thermodynamic stability at high pressure and dynamical stability at ambient pressure indicate that it can be made by the route established for this family.

title: Shadow Molecular Dynamics for General Nonlinear Flexible-Charge Models
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials have greatly expanded the reach of molecular dynamics simulations, but complex chemical environments often require explicit treatment of long-range electronic response, including charge transfer and polarization. Physics-based flexible-charge models capture these effects but require global nonlinear charge equilibration at every time step to obtain Born-Oppenheimer energies and forces. This process is computationally expensive and can lead to instabilities unless tightly converged. Here, we introduce a shadow molecular dynamics framework for flexible-charge models with arbitrary local nonlinearities and long-range multipolar electrostatics. We replace the exact Born-Oppenheimer potential with a nearby shadow potential obtained by exactly equilibrating a partially linearized electronic energy functional. This provides conservative forces and reduces the global nonlinear equilibration to a quasi-diagonal linear problem that can be solved directly at low cost. Auxiliary dynamical electronic degrees of freedom, propagated through an extended-Lagrangian dynamics, capture the long-range electronic response and define the reference state for the linearization of the energy functional. GPU-accelerated simulations with over 100,000 atoms demonstrate that the shadow potential closely follows the tightly converged Born-Oppenheimer surface, while maintaining long-term stability at a computational cost approaching that of a fixed-charge model. These advances establish an efficient and broadly applicable framework for machine-learned interatomic potentials that explicitly incorporate long-range electrostatic interactions and environment-dependent electronic response.

title: Local and itinerant orbital contributions to the gyromagnetic response of paramagnetic metals
abstract: Orbitronics exploits orbital angular momentum to generate and manipulate angular-momentum currents for controlling magnetisation, offering new approaches to magnetic memory and logic. A quantitative description of this process requires establishing how orbital angular momentum contributes to magnetic moments and, consequently, to the gyromagnetic response that governs magnetisation dynamics. Here, we present a first-principles framework for calculating the effective gyromagnetic tensor (g') of paramagnetic metals, consistently incorporating local and itinerant orbital contributions, spin-orbit coupling, and both state- and occupation-change effects. Applying the framework to V and Pt, we find that orbital paramagnetic responses are comparable to or larger than spin contributions and substantially modify g' from the free-electron value. The atom-centered approximation can underestimate the orbital response by approximately a factor of two, while neglecting occupation changes produces significant errors in the calculated g'. Our calculated g' values for V and Pt agree with experiment, while their pronounced dependence on band filling reveals a route to engineering angular-momentum responses through electronic-structure control. The results establish the modern theory of orbital magnetism as an essential ingredient for describing gyromagnetic response and provide a framework for identifying materials with enhanced orbital functionalities.

title: Amplitude-conserving frequency demultiplexer based on a spin wave delay line
abstract: Propagating spin waves have emerged as promising candidates for signal processing and information transmission. We present a theoretical investigation of the generation, propagation and collection of spin-wave wave packets in micrometer-wide magnetic conduits, highlighting their potential for analogue frequency demultiplexing in space and time. We clarify the roles of the excitation duration and of the spin wave dispersion relation, as well as the influence of the spin-wave linewidth in setting the spatio-temporal evolution of propagating spin-wave wavepackets excited by Gaussian field pulses. We issue rules for the spatio-temporal separation of wavepackets that carry different frequencies. We finally propose an amplitude-conserving frequency demultiplexer based on a spin wave delay line of 60x5 $μ$m$^2$ footprint.

title: From Reactive to Agentic Resilience: Multi-Timescale AI-RAN Orchestration Under Signaling Storms
abstract: Next-generation open radio access network (Open RAN) and AI-RAN deployments turn the RAN into a disaggregated, compute-aware platform whose service continuity depends on many control loops acting at different timescales. Resilience in this setting is best seen as a lifecycle spanning anticipation, absorption, adaptation, recovery, and evolution. Yet, existing mechanisms remain stage-specific and are rarely coordinated across the control hierarchy. This paper argues that agentic AI offers an orchestration layer that coordinates this lifecycle, turning operator intent into coordinated action while keeping slow language-model reasoning off the fast control path. Using mass-attachment signaling storms as a running study, we build a discrete-event Open RAN attach simulator that captures retry amplification, shared-compute contention, and non-instantaneous provisioning, and we propose a three-tier framework in which an orchestrator at the service management and orchestration layer sets a standing policy, a per-site non-real-time agent judges storms and anticipates scheduled crowds, and a deterministic near-real-time loop enforces every decision. Across experiments, the agentic controller approaches the resilience of a fully provisioned pool of servers at a quarter of its capacity by reading a scheduled event from a calendar and provisioning ahead of it. No reactive weight setting recovers this once the surge arrives. Free-text operator intents ground into control directives at 94% exact match on previously unseen intents, and a single instruction reshapes live behavior end to end. We also quantify the latency, cost, and contention limits that bound it. The supplementary material provides analytical proof of the derived Theorem on anticipation horizon, as well as the subsequent Corollary results on reactive provisioning limits.

title: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
abstract: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Its 11 projects, spanning financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting, are reconstructed with 13 domain experts from real materials and chain 150 subtasks through 2-15 rounds of new materials and client feedback. Because no reference outputs are injected, agents inherit their own errors from one task to the next. Expert rubrics then score every checkpoint as well as the final package. Across seven model-harness systems, even the best system scores only 65.0 out of 100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. The failures are often failures of carrying work forward: in one audit project, all seven systems addressed the review findings, but only one preserved traceability. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery, which also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

title: Bottom-heaviness stabilizes pelagic fish eggs and generates advective transport at their surface
abstract: Pelagic fish eggs are small spheres (~1 mm) that drift in the open ocean, carried by large-scale currents. Embedded in these currents are egg-scale turbulent eddies that impose local rotational forcing on the eggs. Accordingly, eggs are considered passive tracer particles that move with these eddies, implying that mass transfer of oxygen and waste are controlled only by molecular diffusion. However, eggs are bottom heavy, characterized by a dense embryo and a buoyant oil globule at opposing poles. We hypothesized that such internal structure generates a gravitational restoring torque, stabilizing the egg and generating relative egg-water motion. To test this hypothesis we exposed fish eggs to controlled flows with shear levels typical of upper mixed-layer and estuarine environments, and analyzed their dynamics. Eggs displayed one of two repeatable behaviors: (i) steady orientation, with a near-constant egg angle, and (ii) revolving motion, with egg rotation at time-varying angular speed. Both behaviors generated relative motion between the eggs and the surrounding water. A rigid-body rotational model balancing external flow-induced torque and gravitational restoring torque showed that transitions between these states depend on local flow fields and developmental stage, with older eggs shifting to revolving behavior at lower external fluid torque. Together, these findings suggest that advective transport is important and that diffusion-only models underestimate exchange rates, which are a major component in predicting the effects of environmental factors on embryo survival.

title: The transformer as a candidate canonical cortical microcircuit
abstract: Neuroscience hypothesizes a canonical microcircuit subserving cortical computation across brain systems. In artificial intelligence, neural networks have become a universal computational substrate. Here, we leverage newly available large-scale data and mapping techniques to compare neural network motifs to the brain. We embedded a spectrum of candidate microcircuit architectures within a common spatial macrocircuit, measuring alignment with an extensive battery of cortical signatures. We find that one specific circuit type—the transformer—uniquely captures fine-grained unit-level circuit details, population-level functional maps and neuronal activity patterns, and systems-level wiring efficiency and behavioral demands. The key ingredient enabling the transformer’s success is a learned multiplicative component making relational information available without extensive long-range wiring. These results suggest striking convergence between computational motifs in natural and artificial intelligence.

title: Embracing Phase Transitions to Rationalize the High Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity of Nickel Selenides in Alkaline Electrolytes
abstract: The transformation of electrodeposited NiSe nanocatalysts was studied under oxygen evolution reaction (OER) conditions in alkaline electrolytes by a combination of operando X-ray absorption (XAS) and operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The upper layers of nickel selenides transform into nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide species, which exhibit higher catalytic OER activity than the as-synthesized nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide, as reported previously. The coupled operando XAS and EIS experiments reveal that the Ni3+/Ni4+ transition occurs at lower potentials than the OER, involving a transient phase transformation at the foot of the nickel oxidation peak. Based on these findings and using insights from complementary operando (Raman spectroscopy, scanning flow cell inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry) and ex situ measurements (XAS and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy), a catalytic cycle is proposed within the framework of frustrated phase transitions linking the molecular transformation of substrate and products (H2O/O2) to structural and electronic changes of the solid catalyst (β-Ni(OH)2/β-NiOOH). Specifically, the Ni–O distance of the formed β-NiOOH surface species on top of the NiSe layers elongates, facilitating rapid local transitions between different catalyst phases and oxidation states, which are essential for rapid completion of the catalytic cycle under operando conditions.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Recent advances in optical sensing strategies for uric acid detection
abstract: Uric acid (UA), a byproduct of purine metabolism, serves as a significant biomarker associated with various medical conditions, including gout, renal and cardiac disorders, and metabolic dysfunctions. This paper presents a comprehensive review of recent advancements in optical sensing technologies for UA detection. The various platforms are systematically categorized into colorimetric and fluorometric sensors, with particular emphasis on their detection parameters, such as sensitivity, selectivity, and detection limits, as well as their operational principles. Fluorometric sensors are noted for achieving exceptionally low detection thresholds (in the nanomolar range) and high specificity, whereas colorimetric sensors are recognized for their rapid, visual results and reliable performance in complex sample matrices. Numerous international research efforts have contributed to the development of highly sensitive and selective UA detection technologies. Despite the development of several optical chemosensors (both fluorescent and colorimetric) a systematic classification remains absent. This review highlights the design strategies and molecular recognition mechanisms of various UA chemosensors, particularly those based on small organic molecules. The integration of these sensors into wearable technology or diagnostic platforms could significantly advance personalized medicine and the management of UA-related conditions. The paper concludes by outlining potential future directions for the field, including the deployment of multiplexed sensing systems and the application of machine learning for signal analysis, to advance the development of next-generation UA optical sensors for point-of-care diagnostics and real-time health monitoring.

title: Role of Dynamics and Spin-State Crossover in Metal-Hydride Hydrogen Atom Transfer (MHAT) and Electron Transfer in Transmetalation during Co–Ni Multimetallic Catalyzed Alkene Hydroarylation
abstract: Metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactions involve hydrogen transfer from a transition-metal hydride to an alkene to generate a metal radical and carbon-centered radical pair. These radicals can then either collapse to a metal–alkyl intermediate or separate into solvent-separated radicals. Little is currently known about the factors that control the lifetime of MHAT-generated radical pairs and subsequent reaction pathway selectivity.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Green Composites for Safer and Durable Water Pipelines
abstract: The intensifying water shortage in Algeria makes clear the need of novel, sustainable strategies to protect distribution networks. Current infrastructure struggles with frequent failures, particularly leaks stemming from corrosion or handling damage during transport and installation. High-density polyethylene (HDPE) has become a material of choice because it handles these challenges well; it is cost-efficient, flexible, and tough enough to withstand harsh environments.This work investigates the failure risks of HDPE pipelines manufactured by ITP Alg{é}rie -- Innovation Transformation Polym{è}re. Mechanical tests were performed on HDPE 100 to determine its fundamental properties, including burst tests under internal pressure and load/unload experiments aimed at establishing a material-specific damage law revealed the dominant degradation mechanisms that occur under different operational and environmental conditions. Based on these findings, a predictive numerical model was developed to simulate damage progression and anticipate potential failures in service. This study introduces a unique hybrid composite patch designed for the precise rehabilitation of compromised pipeline sections. It shows strong promise for rebuilding the mechanical integrity of pipes, which is vital for maintaining a safe and long-lasting drinking water supply.

title: Small-Molecule Contacts to NMR-Invisible Aβ40 Oligomers Revealed by Pressure-Jump NMR and t 1-Noise Suppression
abstract: Soluble amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers are widely implicated as neurotoxic species in Alzheimer’s disease but remain difficult to characterize because their transient, heterogeneous assemblies are effectively invisible to conventional solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Hydrostatic pressure (∼2.2 kbar) dissociates Aβ40 oligomers into monomers with sharp, intense resonances. Here, we exploit this pressure-dependent behavior to detect weak intermolecular contacts formed between small molecules and the NMR-invisible oligomers and read them out after pressure-induced dissociation. Using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a simple small-molecule probe, we combine pressure-jump NMR with NOE difference spectroscopy to obtain residue-resolved DMSO-to-Aβ40-oligomer contacts. Because the resulting NOE signals are very weak, their detection requires substantial suppression of t1 noise that is shown to arise primarily from minute FID-to-FID phase and frequency instabilities. We therefore introduced RePAIR (Reference-based Phase And frequency Instability Reduction), a software package that uses an internal reference resonance to correct per-FID phase and frequency errors in gradient-encoded, phase-modulated data sets, suppressing t1 noise and revealing otherwise hidden intermolecular NOEs. The resulting contact profile shows preferential DMSO interactions with the ordered, hydrophobic β-sheet core of the Aβ40 oligomers. More broadly, this approach provides a framework for obtaining residue-resolved information on weak small-molecule interactions with transient protein assemblies that are otherwise inaccessible to conventional solution NMR.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Magnetic order in Co[Cr(CN)$_6$]$_{2/3}\cdot z$H$_2$O and its interplay with correlated vacancy order
abstract: Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) are versatile hybrid framework materials that often exhibit local and long-range departures from their cubic parent structure, influencing their functionality. Long-range magnetic order is common in PBAs, owing to magnetic interactions between transition metal ions via bridging cyanide ligands in the structure. Here we report the magnetic structure of cobalt (II) hexacyanochromate, Co[Cr(CN)$_6$]$_{2/3}\cdot z$H$_2$O, determined using neutron powder diffraction. No evidence for magnetostriction at the magnetic ordering temperature is observed in contrast to the reported behaviour of a related PBA. Following experimental characterisation of the magnetic order of this PBA, we employ a simple Monte Carlo model to gain a better understanding of the relationship between hexacyanometallate vacancy distributions and magnetic ordering behaviour in these materials. This model shows that magnetic ordering is robust to the extent and nature of vacancy correlations, with only minor effects noticeable in the critical region, suggesting that PBAs with the same composition but different vacancy correlations might be expected to show similar magnetic behaviour.

title: GraTED: Graph--Tensor EEG Decoding for Passenger Hazard Perception in Autonomous Vehicles
abstract: Passenger electroencephalography (EEG) can reveal road risk through anticipatory responses before hazardous events and neural reactions around their onset. However, existing EEG decoding methods often map physiologically meaningful arrangement of electrodes onto artificial 2D grids and thus flatten the higher-order time-feature representations into matrices, obscuring meaningful structure in the data. To preserve and exploit the spatial and time-feature structure of EEG recordings, we propose the Graph-Tensor EEG Decoding Model (GraTED) for passenger risk prediction (RP) and danger identification (DI) in autonomous-vehicle scenarios. GraTED models the electrode arrangement as an undirected graph based on their scalp locations, using graph convolution to capture spatial dependencies and low-rank tensor classification to preserve the multidimensional time-feature structure, while controlling model complexity. Evaluated on the PassengerEEG dataset, comprising 11 participants and 45 hours of recordings, GraTED achieves the highest balanced accuracy, compared to the state-of-the-art, across all three evaluation settings, while requiring the fewest learnable parameters among seven baseline methods.

title: RxnMiner: A Multimodal Agent for Structured Reaction Data Extraction from Chemistry Figures
abstract: Reaction data underpin machine learning for reaction prediction, condition recommendation, and retrosynthetic planning, yet extracting these data from literature figures still requires substantial manual effort. Many figures encode multiple experiments through shared templates, substituent tables, and product grids. Recovering concrete reaction records therefore requires molecular recognition, association of evidence with individual experimental entries, and reconstruction of indirectly specified participants. We present RxnMiner, a multimodal agent system that combines an expert-informed extraction procedure with a chemistry toolbox to coordinate these operations. The agent reads molecular structures, resolves shared and entry-specific evidence, and instantiates participants from templates to assemble source-linked reaction records. We also introduce ChemRxn-Bench, a benchmark of 603 reaction figures with 8,547 manually annotated and reviewed reaction records, evaluated under a common protocol for exact molecular identity and reactant-product pairing. On this benchmark, with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as the backbone, RxnMiner raises stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 from 21.0% under direct prediction to 71.0%, compared with 25.0% for the strongest existing extraction system. Across five backbones, it also outperforms the same base agent without the extraction procedure and chemistry toolbox by 9.4 to 25.5 points. Applied without human intervention to 10,107 literature figures, RxnMiner produces a silver corpus of 88,202 source-linked reaction records.

title: Observing oscillations using the non-magnetic and magnetic spin Hall effect in a non-collinear antiferromagnet
abstract: In this study, it was observed that, in non-collinear IrMn3, both the non-magnetic spin Hall effect (NMSHE) and the magnetic spin Hall effect (MSHE) exhibit oscillations as the triangularly ordered magnetic moments of IrMn3 evolve with temperature. These oscillations are strongly influenced by the magnetic properties at the interface between IrMn3 and the adjacent material. Permalloy (Py), a ferromagnet, and platinum (Pt), a paramagnet, were employed as adjacent layers. Such experimental analyses demonstrate the pioneering nature of this phenomenon, which is validated through magnetoresistance measurements performed under different experimental conditions.

title: Superinsulation, electric confinement in condensed matter
abstract: Superinsulation is the confining phase of condensed matter systems. It is a genuine quantum state of matter, dual to superconductivity, just as confinement in particle physics is dual to the Higgs phase. In contrast to hadron physics, the gauge field that becomes confining is not colour SU(3) but the conventional U(1) electromagnetic field. Superinsulation arises in superconductors with an emergent granular condensate when core-less XY vortices between condensate grains become tensionless, unobservable Dirac strings and magnetic monopoles are liberated and condense. This magnetic condensate confines electric fields into flux tubes, strings that generate a linear potential between Cooper pairs. These dual Abrikosov flux tubes give rise to infinite electrical resistance, persisting up to a finite deconfinement temperature. We shall review the theoretical framework of superinsulation together with its experimental validation, including the direct observation of the linear confining potential and we shall stress how phase-only approaches and disorder-based ideas for the phases around the superconductor-to-insulator transition are hard to reconcile with recent experimental observations.

title: Donor−Acceptor Engineering in Porphyrin-Based Two-Dimensional Polymers for Ultrafast Nonlinear Optical Response
abstract: Leveraging their extended π-conjugation, structurally tunable backbones, and superior film-forming processability, two-dimensional (2D) organic polymers have emerged as a highly promising class of materials for third-order nonlinear optical (NLO) applications. Herein, a series of porphyrin-based donor−acceptor (D−A) 2D polymer films, namely, TAPP-TAPZ, TAPP-BATD, TAPP-TDAT, and TAPP-BDTA, are successfully fabricated via a liquid−liquid interfacial polymerization approach.

title: Internal friction and frequency-dependent conductivity in the bivariate site energy model for the mixed alkali effect in glasses
abstract: The mixed alkali effect is fundamental to understanding ion transport in glasses. It manifests itself in strong changes of various ionic transport properties when one type of ion is successively replaced by another type. Recently, we have developed a new theory of thermally activated hopping in bivariate random site energy landscapes that takes into account site occupation statistics according to generalized Fermi distributions and mixture kinetics in accordance with linear irreversible thermodynamics. The theory was successfully applied to predict the behavior of partial conductivities and their activation energies at low frequencies corresponding to the dc limit. Here we show that the theory is capable to capture the salient features of the mixed alkali effect observed in ac ion conductivities and in the peculiar behavior of the internal friction.

title: Sulfotransferase Catalyzed Resolution and Nucleophilic Substitution of Alcohols to Access N-H-Heterocycles
Gas–Water Interfacial Conversion of CO2-Derived Carbamates to Substituted Ureas
abstract: Amines (RNH2) capture carbon dioxide (CO2) in water as carbamates (RNHCO2–), one C–N bond short of a urea (RNHCONHR′). Interfacial studies have so far produced only unsubstituted urea from inorganic nitrogen sources, whereas conversion of organic carbamates to substituted ureas at aqueous interfaces remains unexamined. Here we show that gas–water interfaces (GWIs) promote this downstream step under ambient aqueous conditions.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: FACTO: fast atom-centered tensor operator for accurate and efficient foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials
abstract: High-throughput inference remains a central challenge for equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials. Here we introduce FACTO, an atom-centered equivariant architecture that confines evolving learned state and dense channel mixing to atoms, expressing neighbor interactions as fully fusible reductions. We complement this design with custom register-accumulated aggregation kernels and tensor-core FP32 emulation, accelerating inference while retaining FP32-level energy conservation under emulated arithmetic in molecular dynamics. Comprehensive evaluations on Matbench Discovery, MLIP Arena and MatCalc demonstrate high throughput alongside strong predictive accuracy and physical reliability. On Matbench Discovery, the four FACTO-OAM variants show top-tier performance by overall rank sum among 46 models with complete scores, advancing the accuracy-throughput Pareto frontier. On MLIP Arena, FACTO achieves state- of-the-art stability under extreme heating and compression, alongside high fidelity in hydrogen combustion. On MatCalc, FACTO outperforms the compared baselines in structural and elastic predictions while retaining competitive accuracy for energetic and thermal properties.

title: Integrative network toxicology and machine learning reveal the potential role of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural in exacerbating pulmonary fibrosis
abstract: Background5-Hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF), a ubiquitous furan derivative formed during the thermal processing of carbohydrate-rich foods, represents a widespread dietary exposure. However, its potential contribution to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remains unclear. This study investigated the molecular links between 5-HMF and IPF using an integrated computational and experimental approach.MethodsIPF-related genes were identified through transcriptomic analysis combining differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Candidate targets were obtained by intersecting IPF-associated genes with predicted 5-HMF targets. Functional enrichment analysis, ensemble machine learning, and SHAP interpretation were performed to prioritize candidate targets, while molecular docking was used to explore potential 5-HMF-target interactions. A bleomycin-induced mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis was further used to evaluate the effects of 5-HMF on fibrotic lung injury and the transcriptional expression of prioritized candidate genes.ResultsA total of 1,776 IPF-associated genes and 143 predicted 5-HMF targets were identified, yielding 12 overlapping candidate targets. Enrichment analysis implicated these genes in fibrosis-related pathways, including chemical carcinogenesis-receptor activation and estrogen signaling. Machine learning analysis prioritized seven core targets (CA2, CA4, ESR2, F10, HSP90AA1, PLA2G1B, and PTPRB), all of which accommodated 5-HMF in their orthosteric pockets in blind docking, albeit with weak, non-selective Vina scores (-4.5 to -5.4 kcal/mol). In vivo, 5-HMF significantly exacerbated bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis, as demonstrated by aggravated lung injury, increased collagen deposition, and elevated expression of Hsp90aa1, Pla2g1b, Ca4, F10, Acta2, and Col1a1.ConclusionOur findings suggest that 5-HMF may exacerbate fibrotic lung injury through multiple fibrosis-related molecular targets and pathways. These findings provide preliminary evidence for a potential association between 5-HMF exposure and the aggravation of pulmonary fibrosis, while further studies are required to determine whether 5-HMF can independently initiate fibrotic pathology.

title: A Hybrid Convolutional Recurrent Neural Model for Noise Detection and Automated Calibration of Medical Devices via Molecular Vibration Analysis
abstract: Accurate noise detection and calibration are essential for maintaining the measurement reliability of medical devices. This study proposes a hybrid convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) framework for noise detection and automated calibration of ventilators and electrocardiogram (ECG) machines using molecular vibration analysis. A molecular vibration model was developed to characterize mechanical vibration, electromagnetic interference, and environmental conduction noise, achieving an average noise classification accuracy of 96.2%.

title: Identifying Key Odorant Compounds and Assessing Odor Additivity in Complex Mixtures via Machine Learning: A Multi-Regional Case Study in China
abstract: With the continuous development of industrial parks in China, odor pollution resulting from the extensive use of solvents has become increasingly prominent, making its accurate analysis and effective prevention and control critically important. To identify key odorant compounds in complex mixtures, this study collected 426 air samples from industrial parks in Guangdong and Zhejiang, China and built a database of odor concentrations and chemical compositions. Machine learning (AutoGluon) combined with SHAP interpretability analysis was employed to build an odor concentration prediction model.

title: RangeFinder: Predicting Ligand Property Ranges from Protein Pockets
abstract: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules. Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context.
